summary: The two adopted corrections (M4.36's interrupt-proof pin, M4.37/done-row's mutant-elapsed-vs-margin) are both accurate and an implementer following M4.36 would now succeed. But this round's OTHER edit -- the sentence newly added to M4.35 asserting the lease-release write is interruptible on the backend that exists today -- is false as measured on Java 25: the write LeaseManager.releaseLocked() actually issues is LocalFsBinStore.putIfMatch, whose Files.createTempFile/Files.copy path completes with the interrupt flag set, both when the flag is set on entry and when the interrupt lands mid-write. Only putIfAbsent's explicit FileChannel throws ClosedByInterruptException, and putIfAbsent is not on the release path. The three surviving-mutation claims are carried forward unverified this round, as instructed; nothing in the delta touches the code they describe.

findings.title: M4.35's new 'interruptible ON THE BACKEND THAT EXISTS TODAY' sentence is false for the write the release path actually makes -- measured
findings.failure_scenario: The row states, in the present tense and as if measured: 'That write is interruptible ON THE BACKEND THAT EXISTS TODAY, not only on a future S3 one: LocalFsBinStore.putIfMatch goes through Files.createTempFile and Files.copy(InputStream, Path, ...), and putIfAbsent opens an explicit FileChannel, whose AbstractInterruptibleChannel.begin() throws ClosedByInterruptException when the flag is ALREADY SET on entry ... So the write dies with ClosedByInterruptException'. The write named one clause earlier is releaseLocked()'s, and LeaseManager.releaseLocked (sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/LeaseManager.java:452) issues store.putIfMatch -- never putIfAbsent. Measured on the project toolchain (java 25.0.4, buildSrc languageVersion 25), replaying LocalFsBinStore.putIfMatch's exact syscall sequence (Files.exists, Files.readString of the .v sidecar, Files.createTempFile, Files.copy(InputStream,Path,REPLACE_EXISTING), ATOMIC_MOVE, Files.writeString): (a) with the interrupt flag already set on entry the whole sequence COMPLETES, no exception, flag still set; (b) with a 200 KB body from a slow stream on a virtual thread and the interrupt delivered mid-copy, all 204800 bytes are written and no exception is thrown; (c) Files.newInputStream + readAllBytes (the refreshed()/read() branch of the same method) also completes with the flag set. Only the standalone check of an explicit FileChannel.open(CREATE_NEW,WRITE) + write threw ClosedByInterruptException -- i.e. exactly the putIfAbsent path, which the ACQUIRE uses and the release does not. Consequence for the tests this row will produce: an implementer of M4.35 reads 'the backend that exists today does this' and builds a reproduction against LocalFsBinStore or MemoryBinStore expecting a swallowed ClosedByInterruptException; the release simply succeeds, so either the test cannot be made red at all, or it is quietly rewritten around a hand-built fake delegate while the row still claims the real backend behaves that way -- a test that pins a mechanism the shipped code does not have. Note the previous round's wording ('On an NIO/S3 backend that write dies with ClosedByInterruptException') was hedged to a backend that does not exist and was defensible; this round de-hedged it, and the de-hedge is the false part. The row's CONCLUSION is unaffected -- the second route in the same sentence, 'under lock contention takeOrFail throws at once', is real (BoundedLock.tryLock(bound, NANOSECONDS) throws when the flag is set) and the swallow-and-return-clean outcome stands. Remedy is to restore the hedge or to name putIfAbsent's channel as the acquire-path illustration it is, not as the release write. Reproduce: /tmp/claude-1000/-home-tuong-work-opensearch-bin-ingester/d515e5cf-a206-44e9-a908-fe3c27c05c6f/scratchpad/ic/IC2.java, IC4.java, IC5.java, run with `java IC2.java` etc.

findings.title: M4.36 cites an existing test as precedent for interrupt-proofness that is never exposed to an interrupt
findings.failure_scenario: 'aQUEUEDCallerIsFailedWithoutWaitingForTheLeaseReleaseToFinish already uses an interrupt-insensitive spin for the same reason'. In that test (sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/BatchingSequencerTerminationTest.java:282) the BatchingSequencer is never closed and nothing ever interrupts the committer -- the delegate dies of a simulated OutOfMemoryError -- and the test's own comments give a different reason for the spin: holding the delegate until the second caller is really queued, so B lands behind the batch instead of inside it. A plain CountDownLatch.await() would work perfectly well there. The spin is interrupt-insensitive incidentally, not 'for the same reason', so the sentence offers as a worked precedent something that never demonstrates the property. Low impact only because the operative instruction is stated outright and independently measured one clause earlier (Semaphore.acquireUninterruptibly(): mutation KILLED), so an implementer is not misdirected -- but the citation itself does not support what it is cited for.

carried_forward: Per the round's instruction the three surviving-mutation claims (M4.36's deletion of failAll(drainRemaining(), terminalFailure()) from close(); M4.37(a) terminalFailure()'s message and cause chain; M4.37(b) the catch(Exception)->catch(Throwable) widening) were NOT re-run. They are unchanged in substance from the two rounds that measured them, and nothing in this delta touches the production code they describe -- re-read in the staged bytes of BatchingSequencer.java to confirm that close(), drainForever's finally and terminalFailure() are as the rows say.
verified_ok: M4.36's pin recipe (backlog-notes.md:293) now matches the code and the measurement. The failed phrasing 'on a latch' is gone. The asymmetry is real in the staged bytes: close() runs stop(); committer.interrupt(); BEFORE the join, so an interruptible pin inside the delegate's commitAll unwinds through commitBatch's catch(IOException|RuntimeException) into drainForever's finally, whose own failAll(drainRemaining(), terminalFailure()) frees the queued caller irrespective of the mutation -- CountDownLatch.await() therefore pins nothing and the mutation survives, while acquireUninterruptibly() holds the committer so only close()'s net can free B and the mutation is killed. The retained caveat is also correct: an interrupt landing before close()'s `boolean wasInterrupted = Thread.interrupted()` is cleared there, so join waits the full 10s and reaches the same !stopped branch -- slow, never wrong.

The elapsed-vs-margin framing (backlog-done.md:105 and backlog-notes.md:297) is honest. '~202-211ms across three independent runs' fairly covers 202 (round 8), 203.9 (round-2 test review), 210.6 (round-2 production review); dropping 203,911,796 ns is right, since a per-nanosecond figure implied a repeatability the runs contradict by ~9ms. Against the 300ms floor in theRealClockTimerActuallyWaitsItsInterval the true margin band is 89-98ms and the rows say '~90-100ms' -- the lower end rounds 0.6ms in the optimistic direction, but the rows state the elapsed range and the floor beside it so a reader recomputes it exactly, and the load-bearing arithmetic ('four times the real figure, not twice it': 400/~95) holds. 'THAT IS THE MUTANT'S ELAPSED TIME, NOT THE MARGIN' now labels the quantity correctly in both places.
